creator: Alexander Terp
description:
`print("\d{4}")` prints `\d4`. No error, no warning. `{4}` is a valid interpolation of the integer literal `4`, so the parser is right and the output is wrong - the silent half of the literal-brace problem, and the only part of it that an error-message change cannot reach.

Confirmed on `bin/radd` at 5b02f50c:

```
print("\d{4}")     ->  \d4        silent
print("{0}")       ->  0          silent
print("{true}")    ->  true       silent
print("\d{2,3}")   ->  error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '{2,'
print("\d{2,}")    ->  error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '{2,'
```

So the leak is exactly the single-token quantifier, which is also the most common one in a regex.

**The rule that closes it: interpolating a constant literal is always pointless.** If the value is known at parse time the author would have written it directly, so `{4}`, `{0}`, `{true}`, `{"s"}` carry no information. Flagging them is near-zero false positive and catches the regex case dead on. Multi-part quantifiers already error, so between the two the quantifier hole closes.

Make it a warning rather than a hint. The hint tier is already noisy enough that people skim it - see the checker false-positive card in this column - and a warning that fires on genuinely dead code earns its severity.

The message should name both exits: `\{` and an `r`-string.

Third independent instance of this bug class. The other two live on the main board and should be closed against this: the orphaned card `escaping-interpolation` (a regex constraint `"\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}"` that silently became `\d-\d-\d`), and `RAD-387: regex constraint interpolation exception`. The `bugfixes` board also carries a `\}` escape card in the same family.

---

### Orientation
- The checker is `rts/check/`, which runs over the AST in `rts/rl/` before the interpreter sees anything. `rts` must not import `core`.
- String interpolation nodes come from the tree-sitter grammar via `rts.ConvertCST`, so the interpolated expression is already a typed AST node by the time the checker walks it - no re-parsing needed.

### Where to start
- `rts/check/` - find where expression nodes are visited and add the rule where an interpolation's expression subtree is reachable.
- `rts/rl/errors.go` for the diagnostic code. This is a lint, so it belongs in the 4xxxx validation band. Allocate a new number; codes are never reused, and retired ones keep their number with a `_retired` suffix.
- `core/error_docs/<code>.md` for the user-facing doc. Style guide is `core/error_docs/AGENTS.md`.

### How to verify
- `make build`, then `./bin/radd` against scratch scripts covering `{4}`, `{0}`, `{true}`, `{"s"}`, and negative cases `{x}`, `{1+1}`, `{f()}` which must stay silent.
- Checker snapshots live in `rts/check/snapshots/`. Add cases there and update with `go test ./rts/check/ -run TestCheckSnapshots -update=<path substring>` - the `=` is required, a bare `-update` swallows the next flag.
- `rad docs RAD<code>` should render the new error doc.

### Done when
- The four constant forms warn; `{x}`, `{1+1}` and any non-constant expression do not.
- The message names both `\{` and `r"..."`.
- New code in `rts/rl/errors.go`, doc in `core/error_docs/`, checker snapshots added.
- `make generate` run, and `make verify-generated` passes - `docs-web/docs/reference/errors.md` is generated from the error docs and CI fails on stale output.

### Watch out for
Do not fire on an interpolation whose expression merely *evaluates* to a constant (`{x}` where `x = 4`). The rule is syntactic: the expression node itself is a literal. Anything wider needs const-folding and will produce false positives, which is the failure mode the checker is already being cleaned up for.
title: Flag interpolation of a constant literal
